steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a security paper analyzing how well honeyword-generation algorithms hold up when the attacker already knows the user's passwords from other sites, for both user-chosen and password-manager-generated passwords. End with a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Credential database breaches and the detection delay
- Honeywords as a detection mechanism and their two criteria
- Password reuse and attackers who know passwords from other sites
- This paper: user-chosen passwords and the false-negative/false-positive tension
- Algorithmically generated passwords
- Contributions and code availability

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Breaches
  - widespread, growing problem
  - 2022 Verizon DBIR: credentials one of two most often breached data types; let attackers masquerade as legitimate users
  - breaches = largest source of passwords for credential stuffing
  - credential stuffing -> vast majority of account takeovers
  - detection delay: six to eight months on average (2022 report)
  - window to crack offline, sell or use
- Honeywords
  - Juels and Rivest, nearly a decade ago
  - decoy passwords stored with real ones; entry of honeyword in login -> breach alarm
  - criteria: (i) breaching attacker can't tell real password from honeywords; (ii) non-breaching attacker can't guess honeywords (false alarms)
  - various generation algorithms since (Sec. 3)
- Password reuse
  - users reuse passwords across sites
  - attacker stuffs breached passwords elsewhere to find the real one
  - previous design: one site monitors entry of another site's honeywords
  - but if attacker already has passwords from other sites (breach, phishing), no stuffing needed
  - realistic: July 2020 report, more than 15 billion credentials in cybercriminal marketplaces, more than two per person
- This paper, user-chosen passwords
  - first critical analysis of honeyword generation in this setting
  - honeywords dissimilar to password -> attacker distinguishes it -> high false-negative probability
  - honeywords similar -> easier to guess -> false breach alarm (false positive)
  - systematic analysis: no known algorithm gives good tradeoff
  - two password tweaking techniques from password guessing: slightly lower false negatives, still high false positives
  - unclear any algorithm gets low false negatives + false-positive rate near 0
- Algorithmically generated passwords (password managers)
  - algorithms ignoring how password was generated -> high false negatives
  - user-configured generator spec inferable from exposed passwords -> discard honeywords not fitting
  - most existing algorithms don't guarantee same pattern
  - use password manager to generate honeywords too: not foolproof, many configurations
  - attacker with more passwords can classify configuration better than defender -> more false negatives
- Contributions
  - formalize false-positive / false-negative rates in this model
  - empirical datasets: existing algorithms (+ two adapted ones) have poor tradeoffs; false negatives far above random guessing or false positives far above zero
  - first study of honeywords for algorithmically generated passwords; only relevant for reversibly encrypted databases (hashing is best practice); generators' myriad configurations a pitfall
- Code: https://github.com/zonghaohuang007/honeywords-analysis

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Credential database breaches have been a widespread security problem for a long time and they are only getting more common. The 2022 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts credentials as one of the two types of confidential data that are breached most often, because they are so useful for attackers to masquerade as legitimate users on the system. Credential database breaches are the biggest source of the compromised passwords that are used in credential stuffing campaigns. And credential stuffing campaigns cause the vast majority of account takeovers. The problem is that there is usually a big delay between when a credential database is breached and when this is discovered. A 2022 report estimates the average delay to detect a data breach at six to eight months. This window of vulnerability gives attackers the chance to crack the passwords offline, and then they can sell them or use them directly.

Juels and Rivest suggested a strategy to detect credential database breaches faster nearly a decade ago. The idea is that a site stores decoy passwords, called honeywords, together with the real passwords in its credential database, so if the attacker breaches the database the correct passwords are hidden among the honeywords. If a honeyword is entered in a login attempt the site is alerted to its breach, since the legitimate user doesn't know the honeyword. Since then researchers have proposed various algorithms for generating honeywords (see Sec. 3) that try to meet two central criteria: (i) an attacker who has breached a site's credential database should have difficulty telling the legitimate password for an account apart from the honeywords of that account, and (ii) an attacker who has not breached the database should have difficulty guessing honeywords for an account, because these guesses will cause false breach alarms.

Users tend to reuse passwords across sites (e.g.,) and this is a challenge for honeywords, because an attacker can stuff the breached passwords of an account at other sites where the same user has accounts, and the legitimate password is the one that works at another site. So previous advances in honeyword system designs give a mechanism where one site can monitor for another site's honeywords being entered in local login attempts. But for an account where the attacker can get the user's passwords on other sites (for example by breaching those sites or by phishing the passwords), the attacker probably doesn't need credential stuffing to tell the legitimate password apart from its honeywords. This might seem like a threat model that is unnecessarily challenging, but unfortunately it is realistic: a July 2020 report found more than 15 billion credentials in circulation in cybercriminal marketplaces, which is on average more than two for every person on the planet.

In this paper we do the first critical analysis of honeyword-generation algorithms in this setting, where the attacker knows legitimate passwords at other sites for the users in a database it is targeting. There is reason to think this threat model would be a big challenge for honeyword efficacy when passwords are user-chosen (and not algorithmically generated). If the honeyword-generation algorithm for the targeted database generates honeywords that are all dissimilar from the user-chosen password, then the known password(s) of the same user might let the attacker distinguish the user-chosen password from its honeywords with high probability. Then the false-negative probability (the probability that the site fails to detect the breach) would be high. But if the algorithm generates some honeywords that are similar to the user-chosen password, it might be easier for an attacker who has not breached the database to guess and enter honeywords in login attempts, and this causes a false breach alarm (false positive).

We do a systematic analysis of current honeyword-generation algorithms and quantify this tension, and we show that there seems to be no known algorithm that gives a good tradeoff for accounts with user-chosen passwords. We also applied two password tweaking techniques from password guessing to improve honeyword generation. These two algorithms relieve the tension a bit by giving slightly lower false-negative probability, but they still cause a high false-positive probability. So it is still far from clear that any honeyword-generation algorithm ensures low false-negative probability and also gives adequate resistance to false breach alarms (i.e., a false-positive rate near 0).

- Algorithmically generated passwords (password managers)
  - ignoring how password was generated -> high false negatives
  - generator spec inferable from exposed passwords -> discard non-fitting honeywords; most algorithms don't guarantee same pattern
  - generating honeywords with a password manager: not foolproof (many configurations); attacker with more passwords classifies config better -> more false negatives
- Contributions
  - formalize false-positive/false-negative rates when attacker has same user's passwords elsewhere
  - existing algorithms + two adapted ones: poor tradeoffs (false negatives far above random guessing or false positives far above zero)
  - first study for algorithmically generated passwords (reversibly encrypted databases only); generator configurations a pitfall
- Code: https://github.com/zonghaohuang007/honeywords-analysis

steps.text:
Credential database breaches have been a widespread security problem for a long time and they are only getting more common. And credential stuffing campaigns cause the vast majority of account takeovers. The problem is that there is usually a big delay between when a credential database is breached and when this is discovered. A 2022 report estimates the average delay to detect a data breach at six to eight months. This window of vulnerability gives attackers the chance to crack the passwords offline, and then they can sell them or use them directly.

Juels and Rivest suggested a strategy to detect credential database breaches faster nearly a decade ago. The idea is that a site stores decoy passwords, called honeywords, together with the real passwords in its credential database, so if the attacker breaches the database the correct passwords are hidden among the honeywords. If a honeyword is entered in a login attempt the site is alerted to its breach, since the legitimate user doesn't know the honeyword. Since then researchers have proposed various algorithms for generating honeywords (see Sec. 3) that try to meet two central criteria: (i) an attacker who has breached a site's credential database should have difficulty telling the legitimate password for an account apart from the honeywords of that account, and (ii) an attacker who has not breached the database should have difficulty guessing honeywords for an account, because these guesses will cause false breach alarms.

Users tend to reuse passwords across sites (e.g.,) and this is a challenge for honeywords, because an attacker can stuff the breached passwords of an account at other sites where the same user has accounts, and the legitimate password is the one that works at another site. So previous advances in honeyword system designs give a mechanism where one site can monitor for another site's honeywords being entered in local login attempts. But for an account where the attacker can get the user's passwords on other sites (for example by breaching those sites or by phishing the passwords), the attacker probably doesn't need credential stuffing to tell the legitimate password apart from its honeywords. This might seem like a threat model that is unnecessarily challenging, but unfortunately it is realistic: a July 2020 report found more than 15 billion credentials in circulation in cybercriminal marketplaces, which is on average more than two for every person on the planet.

In this paper we do the first critical analysis of honeyword-generation algorithms in this setting, where the attacker knows legitimate passwords at other sites for the users in a database it is targeting. There is reason to think this threat model would be a big challenge for honeyword efficacy when passwords are user-chosen (and not algorithmically generated). If the honeyword-generation algorithm for the targeted database generates honeywords that are all dissimilar from the user-chosen password, then the known password(s) of the same user might let the attacker distinguish the user-chosen password from its honeywords with high probability. Then the false-negative probability (the probability that the site fails to detect the breach) would be high. But if the algorithm generates some honeywords that are similar to the user-chosen password, it might be easier for an attacker who has not breached the database to guess and enter honeywords in login attempts, and this causes a false breach alarm (false positive).

We do a systematic analysis of current honeyword-generation algorithms and quantify this tension, and we show that there seems to be no known algorithm that gives a good tradeoff for accounts with user-chosen passwords. We also applied two password tweaking techniques from password guessing to improve honeyword generation. These two algorithms relieve the tension a bit by giving slightly lower false-negative probability, but they still cause a high false-positive probability. So it is still far from clear that any honeyword-generation algorithm ensures low false-negative probability and also gives adequate resistance to false breach alarms (i.e., a false-positive rate near 0).

Then we look at accounts with algorithmically generated passwords, like those a password manager might generate. The critical finding here is that honeyword-generation algorithms that don't take into account how the legitimate password was generated will give high false-negative probability. For example, if the user has a password manager that generates passwords to fit a specification the user configured, and the exposed passwords of that user let the attacker infer this specification, then the attacker can throw away any honeywords that don't fit that pattern. We will quantify how well the adversary can do this against existing honeyword-generation algorithms, and most of them don't guarantee honeywords with the same pattern as the legitimate password. Then we consider the possibility that the honeyword-generation algorithm itself uses a password manager to generate honeywords whenever the user does. But because users might adopt many different generator configurations, this is not foolproof. In particular, if the attacker knows potentially more passwords of the same user's accounts elsewhere, it can classify the typical configuration of the user better than the defender can. This advantage means more false negatives, which we will show in certain cases.

To summarize, our contributions are:

- • We formalize the false-positive and false-negative rates of honeywords in a model where the attacker has passwords for the same user at other sites (for example by breaching those sites or phishing the user).

- • With these definitions and empirical datasets of compromised passwords, we show that existing honeyword-generation algorithms (and two honeyword-generation methods we adapted from password-guessing attacks) have poor tradeoffs between false negatives and false positives in this threat model. All the methods we analyzed have a false-negative rate much higher than random guessing (i.e., false-negative attackers can often easily distinguish the account password from honeywords) or a false-positive rate much higher than zero (i.e., false-positive attackers can often easily cause false breach alarms).

- • We do the first study of using honeywords to protect algorithmically generated passwords. This is only relevant for sites that reversibly encrypt their password databases (because password hashing, which is best practice, should make algorithmically generated passwords irrecoverable for an attacker who breaches the database), but our study gives interesting findings in this setting. With passwords gathered from popular password managers, we show that adding honeywords without paying attention to whether the account's password is algorithmically generated gives little protection for existing honeyword-generation algorithms. We also explore using automatic password generators to generate honeywords when the account password is identified as algorithmically generated itself, but we find that the myriad configurations of these generators can be a pitfall for honeyword generation.

The source code for our experiments is available from https://github.com/zonghaohuang007/honeywords-analysis.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Credential database breaches have long been a widespread security problem, and they are only becoming more so. The 2022 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report places credentials among the two most often breached types of confidential data, since they are so useful for attackers seeking to masquerade as legitimate users on the system [1]. Credential database breaches are the largest source of compromised passwords used in credential stuffing campaigns [2], and credential stuffing campaigns in turn cause the vast majority of account takeovers [3]. Unfortunately, there is usually a significant delay between the breach of a credential database and its discovery: a 2022 report estimates the average delay to detect a data breach at six to eight months [4]. This window of vulnerability gives attackers the opportunity to crack the passwords offline and then sell or leverage them directly [2,3].

A strategy to accelerate the detection of credential database breaches, suggested by Juels and Rivest nearly a decade ago [5], is for a site to store decoy passwords, or honeywords, alongside real passwords in its credential database, so that if an attacker breaches the database, the correct passwords are hidden among the honeywords. Entry of a honeyword in a login attempt then alerts the site to its breach, since the legitimate user does not know the honeyword. Since this proposal, researchers have proposed various algorithms for generating honeywords (see Sec. 3) to meet two central criteria: (i) it should be difficult for an attacker who has breached a site’s credential database to distinguish an account’s legitimate password from its honeywords, and (ii) it should be difficult for an attacker who has not breached the database to guess an account’s honeywords, since such guesses will induce false breach alarms.

Users’ tendency to reuse passwords across sites (e.g., [6,7]) presents a challenge for honeywords: an attacker can stuff an account’s breached passwords at other sites where the same user has accounts, discovering the legitimate password as the one that works elsewhere. Previous advances in honeyword system designs [8] therefore provide a mechanism by which one site can monitor for the entry of another site’s honeywords in local login attempts. However, for an account whose user’s passwords on other sites the attacker can obtain (e.g., by breaching those sites or by phishing), the attacker will likely not need credential stuffing to differentiate the legitimate password from its honeywords. While this threat model might seem unnecessarily challenging, it is unfortunately realistic: a July 2020 report found more than 15 billion credentials in circulation in cybercriminal marketplaces [9], an average of more than two for every person on the planet.

In this paper we conduct the first critical analysis of honeyword-generation algorithms in this setting, i.e., where the attacker knows legitimate passwords at other sites for the users represented in the database it targets. There is reason to suspect that this threat model poses significant challenges to honeyword efficacy for user-chosen (versus algorithmically generated) passwords. On the one hand, if the honeyword-generation algorithm populating the targeted database generates honeywords that are all dissimilar from the user-chosen password, the known password(s) for the same user might let the attacker distinguish the user-chosen password from its honeywords with high probability, making the false-negative probability (the probability that the site fails to detect the breach) high. On the other hand, if the algorithm generates some honeywords similar to the user-chosen password, this might make it easier for an attacker who has not breached the database to guess and enter honeywords in login attempts, thereby inducing a false breach alarm (false positive).

Through a systematic analysis of current honeyword-generation algorithms, we quantify this tension and show that there appears to be no known algorithm providing a good tradeoff for accounts with user-chosen passwords. We additionally applied two password tweaking techniques from password guessing to improve honeyword generation. While these two algorithms relieve the tension by providing slightly lower false-negative probability, they still induce a high false-positive probability. It therefore remains far from clear that any honeyword-generation algorithm ensures low false-negative probability while providing adequate resistance to false breach alarms (i.e., a false-positive rate near 0).

We then turn to accounts with algorithmically generated passwords, such as those generated by a password manager. The critical finding in this case is that honeyword-generation algorithms that ignore the method by which the legitimate password was generated yield high false-negative probability. For example, if the user employs a password manager that generates passwords to fit a user-configured specification, and the passwords exposed for that user let the attacker infer this specification, the attacker can discard any honeywords not fitting that pattern. We quantify the adversary’s ability to do so against existing honeyword-generation algorithms, most of which do not guarantee honeywords of the same pattern as the legitimate password. We then consider having the honeyword-generation algorithm itself leverage a password manager to generate honeywords whenever the user does. Due to the numerous generator configurations users might adopt, however, this is not foolproof. In particular, if the attacker knows potentially more passwords for the same user’s accounts elsewhere, it can classify the user’s typical configuration better than the defender can, implying an increase in false negatives, which we demonstrate in certain cases.

To summarize, our contributions are as follows:

- • We formalize the false-positive and false-negative rates of honeywords in a model in which the attacker possesses passwords for the same user at other sites (obtained, e.g., by breaching those sites or phishing the user).

- • Using these definitions and empirical datasets of compromised passwords, we show that existing honeyword-generation algorithms (and two honeyword-generation methods adapted from password-guessing attacks) exhibit poor tradeoffs between false negatives and false positives in this threat model. All analyzed methods have either a false-negative rate much higher than random guessing (i.e., false-negative attackers can often easily distinguish the account password from honeywords) or a false-positive rate much higher than zero (i.e., false-positive attackers can often easily induce false breach alarms).

- • We conduct the first study of using honeywords to protect algorithmically generated passwords. Although this is relevant only for sites that reversibly encrypt their password databases (since password hashing, the best practice, should render algorithmically generated passwords irrecoverable to an attacker who breaches the database), our study yields interesting findings in this setting. Using passwords gathered from popular password managers, we show that introducing honeywords without attention to whether the account’s password is algorithmically generated offers little protection for existing honeyword-generation algorithms. We further explore using automatic password generators to generate honeywords when the account password is identified as algorithmically generated, but find that the myriad configurations of these generators can be a pitfall for honeyword generation.
